Chapter 2. How Fairy Tales Help Children Face Fear and Darkness.
Every kid, sooner or later, wrestles with fears that feel way too big to put into words. Maybe it's shadows lurking in the corner, or that stomach-churning worry of being left alone. Sometimes it's just the nagging thought that something bad could happen. These feelings are all part of growing up.
Now, grown-ups often want to keep children safe from anything scary. They look for stories that are soft, gentle, maybe even a bit sugary. But fairy tales? They take a much bolder approach. Instead of hiding the darkness, they bring it right out into the open—giving it shape and substance, so it can actually be faced.
Picture a child who's terrified of being abandoned. The story of Hansel and Gretel jumps right into that fear: two kids, lost in the woods, forced to fend for themselves. The story doesn’t gloss over their fear or the danger lurking all around. Instead, it lets the listener feel those emotions—but in a space that’s safe and controlled. The dark forest turns into a symbol for all those unknowns in life, and the witch’s house? That’s the temptation and threat that can show up when you least expect it.
As you follow the story, you notice something important. The children don’t just sit around and wait for a miracle. They use their smarts, their courage, and a whole lot of creativity to get out of trouble. For the child listening, this isn’t just a thrilling adventure—it’s a lesson in resilience. It shows that fear isn’t something to run from or pretend doesn’t exist. It’s something you can face, work through, and even overcome.
A lot of adults worry that telling these stories will make kids even more anxious. But you know what? The opposite usually happens. When children hear about monsters, witches, or evil stepmothers, they pick up on echoes of their own worries. Suddenly, those vague, shadowy fears have a face and a name. And when the hero or heroine wins in the end, there’s a real sense of relief—and a spark of empowerment. The message is quiet but strong: even the scariest problems can be beaten.
There’s often a moment after the story’s done, when a child is lying in bed, replaying what they’ve heard. The images linger—the dark woods, the glowing fire, the clever getaway. But instead of feeling powerless, the child starts to feel that, maybe, they have what it takes to face their own fears, too. The story’s given them a way to process those feelings—to see that, yes, danger is real, but it doesn’t have to win.
Fairy tales don’t pretend that life is always easy, or that there’s never pain or loss. They admit that things can get tough, and bad stuff does happen. But they also show that courage, clever thinking, and kindness can make all the difference. In a way, these tales become practice for real life, helping kids build the emotional tools they’ll need as they grow up.
